name: Elderton Shiraz Single Vineyard Command 2014
text:
## Elderton Shiraz Single Vineyard Command 2014

**The story.** Elderton's home vineyard sits on the banks of the North Para River in [Nuriootpa](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Elderton+Wines,+Nuriootpa,+South+Australia,+Australia&t=k), in the [Barossa Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barossa_Valley_wine_region). The estate says it was planted in 1894 by early German settlers, the Scholz family, and bought in 1916 by Samuel Elderton Tolley, who named it Elderton and sold the fruit to his family's winery. It fell derelict in the early years of the vine pull, around 1975 ([Elderton](https://eldertonwines.com.au/pages/about-elderton-wines)). Accounts of the dates differ: Wikipedia credits Tolley with the 1894 planting, and Wine Spectator gives 1900 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elderton_Wines); [Wine Spectator](https://www.winespectator.com/articles/command-performance-at-elderton-14888)).

Then came an extraordinary offer to Neil and Lorraine Ashmead, newly back from the Middle East: "If you buy the house, I will give you the surrounding 72 acres of old vines for nothing." The family restored the vineyard, made its first wine in 1982, won Australia's [Jimmy Watson Memorial Trophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Watson_Memorial_Trophy) in 1993, and in 2000 the World's Best Shiraz trophy in London ([Elderton](https://eldertonwines.com.au/pages/about-elderton-wines); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elderton_Wines)). Their sons Cameron and Allister have run Elderton since 2003, with winemaker Richard Langford.

**The wine: Command.** Command is Elderton's flagship, from the Command block of the home vineyard, first made in 1988 ([Wine Spectator](https://www.winespectator.com/articles/command-performance-at-elderton-14888)). The block lies on deep alluvial silt over red and brown earth and limestone, with rows unusually planted east-west, which lets cooling breezes from the Barossa Ranges flow along the rows ([Nicks Wine Merchants](https://www.nicks.com.au/products/2014-elderton-command-shiraz)). The old vines give only about half a tonne per acre. The five parcels are hand-picked over five weeks, fermented in open concrete vats, finished in new French and American oak puncheons, aged about 30 months in barrel and a further year in bottle ([Wine Access](https://www.wineaccess.com/catalog/2014-elderton-command-single-vineyard-shiraz-barossa-valley_b73598ee-b8f7-4367-87fa-8001ccdbfeb1); [Elderton](https://eldertonwines.com.au/products/2015-command-shiraz)).

Wine Spectator has twice put Command in its Top 100, with the 1995 and 2000 ([Wine Spectator](https://www.winespectator.com/articles/command-performance-at-elderton-14888)). Halliday's Wine Companion found the 2014 shows "Elderton's newfound restraint".

**The vintage.** [Jancis Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jancis_Robinson)'s [South Australia vintage chart](https://www.jancisrobinson.com/learn/vintages/south-australia) says 2014 saw "everything from frost to high winds to heatwaves", with yields lower than usual; "nobody is claiming it is a great vintage", but quality was generally reliable. The critics loved the 2014 all the same.

**What the critics say for 2014.**
- **Ned Goodwin, [James Halliday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Halliday_%28writer%29)'s Wine Companion: 97** (as listed by [Nicks](https://www.nicks.com.au/products/2014-elderton-command-shiraz)). "Hewn of 1894 ancient vine oomph and tannin management of aplomb, this is power corseted by a filmy, gossamer texture and sheer, strident vinosity." The wine "could come from nowhere else": dark fruit, anise, tar, camphor and "a Cadbury milk chocolate creaminess", with sensitive oak. Drink by 2040.
- **[Wine Advocate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wine_Advocate): 96** (as listed by [Wine Access](https://www.wineaccess.com/catalog/2014-elderton-command-single-vineyard-shiraz-barossa-valley_b73598ee-b8f7-4367-87fa-8001ccdbfeb1)). Aged in French and American oak, 80% new: smoky campfire, vanilla and raspberry; full-bodied, lush, creamy and concentrated, with a crisp, fruit-driven finish. "Quintessential Barossa Shiraz."
- **Nicks Wine Merchants: 98** (March 2018), the retailer's own score: "old school Elderton Command at its best", dense and voluptuous, with "cashmere like tannins". "Sexy is back."
- **[CellarTracker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CellarTracker) community: 92.4** (from your CellarTracker list).

**How it's drinking now.** In October 2026 the wine is twelve years old. Your CellarTracker list gives a window of 2023 to 2035, and Halliday's to 2040. So it is in its prime. Wine Access describes it with tar, braised meat, blackberry and fig paste, black olive and camphor, and recommends "a good hour aeration". Decant it for an hour.

**Food.** Big Barossa Shiraz wants big flavours: a charred rib eye, slow-cooked [brisket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brisket), braised beef short ribs, or the Barossa's own smoked [mettwurst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mettwurst). Hard aged cheddar works too.

**Value and where to buy.** BSW Liquor carries a recent Command, the 2021, at $110 (listed under Ashmead Family Vintners, the family company since 2024).

**From the history books**
- **A misspelled valley.** Colonel [William Light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Light) named the valley in 1837 after the [Battle of Barrosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Barrosa) in Spain, where he had fought in 1811; a clerical error registered it as "Barossa" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barossa_Valley_wine_region)).
- **Three ships to Silesia.** In 1841 the South Australian Company chartered three ships to Silesia offering refuge and land to settlers; nearly 500 families came, and found the warm valley ideal for vines, though Silesia had almost no winemaking tradition ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barossa_Valley_wine_region)).
- **From port to Shiraz.** For decades the Barossa made mainly fortified "port-style" wines, and in the mid-20th century it was seen as an inferior region, with its old Shiraz vines used in anonymous blends. In the 1980s, small family producers of old-vine Shiraz won international acclaim, and Jancis Robinson came to call the Barossa "Australia's quintessential wine region" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barossa_Valley_wine_region)).
- **Protected by law.** To stop the valley turning into a suburb of [Adelaide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adelaide), South Australia passed the Character Preservation (Barossa Valley) Act in 2012 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barossa_Valley_wine_region)).

**Curious details**
- **Free vines.** The Ashmeads were offered the 72 acres of old vines "for nothing" if they bought the house ([Elderton](https://eldertonwines.com.au/pages/about-elderton-wines)).
- **Houses all around.** Housing subdivisions now surround the vineyard on the edge of Nuriootpa, but the family "steadfastly refuses to give in and sell" ([Wine Spectator](https://www.winespectator.com/articles/command-performance-at-elderton-14888)).
- **Learning to be Barossan.** Alister Ashmead told Wine Spectator: "It was only in the late 1980s that we realized that we were all individuals and that we didn't have to be like everyone else in the world", when Barossa winemakers stopped picking early to imitate European reds ([Wine Spectator](https://www.winespectator.com/articles/command-performance-at-elderton-14888)).
